lessons.title: Greetings and Etiquette in Equatorial Guinea
lessons.body: In Equatorial Guinea, greetings are not just politeâthey are a necessary first step before any business discussion. When you meet someone, always start with a handshake. For a more formal setting, use the title 'Don' for men and 'DoÃ±a' for women, followed by their first name or surname. For example, 'Buenos dÃ­as, Don Juan' or 'Buenas tardes, DoÃ±a MarÃ­a.' If you are meeting a group, greet each person individually. Skipping someone is considered disrespectful. In rural areas, a handshake may be followed by a light touch on the forearmâthis shows warmth. In Malabo or Bata, business meetings often begin with a few minutes of small talk about family, health, or the weather. Avoid jumping straight to business; that is seen as pushy. Use 'usted' (formal you) until invited to use 'tÃº.' If someone says 'tutÃ©ame,' you can switch. Punctuality is valued in formal meetings, but be prepared to wait 10â15 minutes for local counterparts. If you are the visitor, arrive on time. When entering a room, greet the most senior person first. At the end of a meeting, thank everyone individually and say 'Mucho gusto' (nice to meet you). A common phrase for goodbye is 'Hasta luego' (see you later), even if you may not meet again soon. In Equatorial Guinea, using Spanish greetings correctly shows respect and opens doors. Practice these phrases daily: 'Â¿CÃ³mo estÃ¡ usted?' (How are you?), 'Muy bien, gracias' (Very well, thanks), and 'Â¿Y su familia?' (And your family?). These small efforts go a long way.

lessons.title: Business Customs in Spanish-Speaking Africa
lessons.body: Equatorial Guinea is the only Spanish-speaking country in Africa, so its business customs blend Spanish and African traditions. Meetings often start with an agenda, but flexibility is key. In government offices, decisions can take weeks or months. For example, a permit that takes 3 days in Nairobi might take 3 weeks in Malabo. Build in buffer time. Business cards are exchanged, but not as formally as in Asia. Present your card with your right hand or both hands. Itâs fine to give it at the start or end of a meeting. Dress code is conservative: men wear suits and ties in Malabo; women wear dresses or skirts below the knee. In Bata, a shirt and trousers are acceptable for men. Hierarchy matters. Always address the most senior person first. In meetings, the boss may speak last, after everyone else has contributed. Avoid interrupting. Negotiations are often relationship-based. You may be invited to share a meal before discussing prices. Accepting shows respect. When discussing contracts, be clear but not aggressive. Use phrases like 'Entiendo su posiciÃ³n' (I understand your position) and 'Â¿Podemos llegar a un acuerdo?' (Can we reach an agreement?). Email is common, but phone calls and WhatsApp are preferred for quick follow-ups. In Equatorial Guinea, many business people use WhatsApp for voice notes. Keep messages short. If you need to schedule a meeting, call first rather than email. For invoices, include all details in Spanish. Payment delays are common; follow up politely every week. A good phrase: 'Le recuerdo amablemente el pago pendiente' (I kindly remind you of the pending payment).

lessons.title: Building Trust and Relationships
lessons.body: In Equatorial Guinea, trust is built through personal connections, not just contracts. Before you talk business, invest time in getting to know your counterpart. A common approach is to share a meal or coffee. For example, invite your contact to a cafÃ© in Malabo for a 'cafÃ© con leche' and talk about family, football, or music. Avoid politics. Ask about their children or hometown. In Equatorial Guinea, family is central. If you remember names of their family members, that shows you care. Another way to build trust is to attend local eventsâchurch services, community meetings, or cultural festivals like the Bata Cultural Week. Showing up shows respect. Gift-giving is part of trust-building, but keep it modest. A small gift like a notebook with your company logo or a box of chocolates is fine. Avoid expensive gifts, which can be seen as bribes. In business, be consistent. If you promise to send a document by Friday, send it by Friday. If you cannot, call and explain. Reliability builds trust. Use 'nosotros' (we) instead of 'yo' (I) to show you see the relationship as a partnership. When you make a mistake, apologize sincerely: 'Lo siento mucho, fue mi error' (I am very sorry, it was my mistake). Also, be patient. Trust takes time. A first meeting may be just to get to know you. A second meeting may include a tour of their facility. By the third or fourth meeting, you may discuss business. Do not rush. In Equatorial Guinea, a handshake and a smile go a long way, but a shared meal goes further.

lessons.title: Gift-Giving and Hospitality Norms
lessons.body: Gift-giving in Equatorial Guinea is a gesture of respect, not a transaction. When you are invited to someoneâs home, bring a small gift for the host. Good options: a bag of rice (5 kg), a bottle of juice, or a box of pastries. Avoid alcohol unless you know the person drinks. In business settings, gifts are usually exchanged after a successful meeting or during holidays. A calendar, a pen set, or a company-branded USB drive is appropriate. Do not give gifts that are too personal, like clothing, unless you know the person well. Also, avoid gifts with sharp edges (knives, scissors) as they symbolize cutting ties. When you receive a gift, open it in front of the giver and say 'Muchas gracias' (Thank you very much). If you are offered food or drink, accept it. Refusing can be seen as rejection. In Equatorial Guinea, hospitality is generous. If you visit a home, you may be offered a meal even if you just ate. Take at least a small portion. Use your right hand to eat if you are eating with your hands. During meals, wait for the host to start. Compliment the food: 'EstÃ¡ delicioso' (Itâs delicious). If you are the host, offer food and drinks multiple times. It is polite to insist. For business lunches, the host usually pays. If you are the guest, offer to pay, but expect the host to insist. If you are the host, pay discreetly. Tipping is not common in Equatorial Guinea, but rounding up the bill is appreciated. In hotels, 500â1000 CFA francs (about $1â2) per bag is fine. Remember, gifts and hospitality are about building a relationship, not about the value.

lessons.title: Taboos and Sensitivities in Business Settings
lessons.body: In Equatorial Guinea, certain topics and behaviors are considered taboo in business. Avoid discussing politics, especially about the president or the ruling party. Also, do not criticize the government or compare Equatorial Guinea to other African countries. Religion is another sensitive topic; while many are Catholic, do not assume. It is fine to ask 'Â¿Es usted religioso?' (Are you religious?) but only if you have a close relationship. In business meetings, avoid pointing with your index finger; use your whole hand. Also, do not use your left hand to give or receive items. The left hand is considered unclean. When sitting, do not show the soles of your feet to someone. Cross your legs at the ankle, not the knee, if you are in a formal setting. Avoid touching someoneâs head; it is seen as disrespectful. In terms of dress, do not wear shorts or flip-flops to a business meeting. Women should avoid very short skirts or low-cut tops. Men should not wear hats indoors. When speaking, avoid direct criticism. Use indirect language. For example, instead of 'You are wrong,' say 'Perhaps we can look at this from another angle.' Do not raise your voice or show anger; it is seen as weakness. Also, avoid making promises you cannot keep. In Equatorial Guinea, a personâs word is their bond. If you break it, you lose trust. Finally, be careful with humor. Sarcasm is not well understood. Stick to friendly, neutral topics like sports or food. If you accidentally offend someone, apologize immediately and sincerely. A simple 'PerdÃ³n, no quise ofender' (Sorry, I didnât mean to offend) can repair the relationship.

lessons.title: Practice: Compare Cultural Norms with Your Own
lessons.body: Now itâs time to practice. This lesson helps you compare Equatorial Guinean business culture with your own. First, make a list of greetings in your culture. How do you greet a senior person? In Equatorial Guinea, you use 'Don' or 'DoÃ±a' and a handshake. In your culture, maybe you bow or use a title. Write down three differences. Next, think about gift-giving. In Equatorial Guinea, a small gift like rice or pastries is common. In your culture, what do you give? Is it money, wine, or something else? Write a sentence in Spanish: 'En mi cultura, damos ______' (In my culture, we give ______). Then, consider taboos. In Equatorial Guinea, you avoid politics and using the left hand. What are taboos in your culture? For example, in some cultures, you donât give clocks or umbrellas. Write two taboos from your culture and two from Equatorial Guinea. Use Spanish phrases: 'En Guinea Ecuatorial, es tabÃº ______' (In Equatorial Guinea, itâs taboo to ______). Now, role-play. Find a partner or imagine a meeting. Greet each other in Spanish using formal 'usted.' Exchange business cards. Discuss a simple business deal. After the role-play, ask: What felt natural? What felt strange? Write a short reflection in Spanish: 'Me sentÃ­ cÃ³modo cuando ______' (I felt comfortable when ______). Finally, create a personal action plan. List three things you will do differently when interacting with Equatorial Guinean business people. For example: 'UsarÃ© usted hasta que me inviten a tutear' (I will use usted until invited to use tÃº). 'LlevarÃ© un regalo pequeÃ±o a la primera reuniÃ³n' (I will bring a small gift to the first meeting). 'EvitarÃ© hablar de polÃ­tica' (I will avoid talking about politics). Practice these with a friend. The more you practice, the more natural it becomes.

quiz.q: What is the formal way to address a man in Equatorial Guinea?
quiz.explanation: In Equatorial Guinea, 'Don' is used as a formal title before a man's first name or surname.

quiz.q: How should you greet a group of people in Equatorial Guinea?
options: D) Shake hands with the oldest person only
quiz.explanation: Greeting each person individually shows respect and is expected in Equatorial Guinean culture.

quiz.q: What is a common small talk topic before business in Equatorial Guinea?
quiz.explanation: Family is a safe and common topic for building rapport before business discussions.

quiz.q: When should you switch from 'usted' to 'tÃº'?
options: C) When invited to do so
quiz.explanation: You should wait until the other person invites you to use 'tÃº' to show respect.

quiz.q: How long might a permit take in Malabo compared to Nairobi?
quiz.explanation: In Malabo, permits can take up to 3 weeks, while in Nairobi they might take 3 days.

quiz.q: What is the preferred dress code for men in Malabo?
quiz.explanation: In Malabo, men are expected to wear suits and ties for business meetings.

quiz.q: In meetings, who often speaks last?
quiz.explanation: In Equatorial Guinean business culture, the most senior person often speaks last after everyone else.

quiz.q: What communication tool is preferred for quick follow-ups?
quiz.explanation: WhatsApp is widely used for quick business communications in Equatorial Guinea.

quiz.q: How often should you follow up on a pending payment?
quiz.explanation: Politely following up weekly is recommended to remind about pending payments.

quiz.q: What is a good way to build trust before business?
quiz.explanation: Sharing a meal helps build personal connections and trust.

quiz.q: Which topic should you avoid in conversation?
quiz.explanation: Politics is a sensitive topic and should be avoided in business settings.

quiz.q: What is a modest gift to bring to a host's home?
quiz.explanation: A bag of rice is a practical and respectful gift in Equatorial Guinea.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid giving sharp objects as gifts?
quiz.explanation: Sharp objects like knives symbolize cutting the relationship, so they are avoided.

quiz.q: What should you do when offered food in a home?
options: C) Ask for a different dish
quiz.explanation: Accepting food shows respect and appreciation for the host's hospitality.

quiz.q: Who usually pays for a business lunch?
quiz.explanation: In Equatorial Guinea, the host typically pays for business meals.

quiz.q: What is a common tipping practice in Equatorial Guinea?
quiz.explanation: Tipping is not standard, but rounding up the bill is appreciated.

quiz.q: Which hand should you use to give or receive items?
quiz.explanation: The right hand is considered clean and should be used for giving or receiving.

quiz.q: What is considered disrespectful when sitting?
quiz.explanation: Showing the soles of your feet is considered disrespectful in Equatorial Guinean culture.

quiz.q: How should you handle a mistake you made?
quiz.explanation: A sincere apology helps maintain trust and respect.

quiz.q: What is a good phrase to use when you don't understand?
quiz.explanation: 'No entiendo' means 'I don't understand' and is polite and clear.

quiz.q: In the practice lesson, what should you compare?
quiz.explanation: The lesson asks you to compare greetings, gift-giving, and taboos between cultures.

quiz.q: What is a good action plan item?
quiz.explanation: Using 'usted' until invited to switch shows respect and is a good practice.

quiz.q: What does 'Mucho gusto' mean?
quiz.explanation: 'Mucho gusto' is a common phrase meaning 'Nice to meet you'.

quiz.q: What is a common phrase for goodbye?
quiz.explanation: 'Hasta luego' means 'See you later' and is commonly used for goodbye.

quiz.q: What is a good topic for small talk?
quiz.explanation: The weather is a neutral and safe topic for small talk.

quiz.q: How many lessons are in this module?
quiz.explanation: The module contains 6 lessons as listed.

quiz.q: What is the capital of Equatorial Guinea?
quiz.explanation: Malabo is the capital city of Equatorial Guinea.

quiz.q: What is a common gift for a business contact?
quiz.explanation: A pen set is a modest and appropriate business gift.

quiz.q: What should you avoid when speaking?
quiz.explanation: Direct criticism can cause loss of face; use indirect language instead.
